assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Anaerobic cell respiration
items.clue: Respiration that does not use oxygen.

items.label: Respiratory substrate
items.clue: A carbon compound whose oxidation releases energy for ATP production.

items.label: Nucleotide
items.clue: A molecule made of a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and one or more phosphate groups.

items.label: Mitochondrion
items.clue: The organelle in which the oxygen-requiring stages of aerobic cell respiration take place, releasing most of the ATP that a eukaryotic cell produces.

questions.stem: Which statement about ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is correct?

options.text: It is a nucleotide: adenine and ribose joined to a chain of three phosphate groups.
It is a small protein that binds energy released from glucose in respiration.
It is the cell's main long-term reserve of energy, built up like glycogen.
It is destroyed once used and is rebuilt from glucose rather than from ADP.

questions.explanation: ATP is a nucleotide made of the base adenine, the pentose sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. It is the molecule that distributes energy within cells.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a life process that ATP supplies with energy?

options.text: Water entering a root hair cell by osmosis uses ATP to cross the membrane against its gradient.
Joining amino acids into a polypeptide releases energy, which the cell holds as ATP.
Pumping sodium ions out of a neuron against their concentration gradient uses ATP directly.
Chromosomes move to the poles in mitosis without ATP, pulled by spindle fibres as they get shorter.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the substrates of cell respiration?

options.text: Only glucose can be respired, because it is the reactant in the equation for respiration.
Glucose and fatty acids are the main substrates, but many other carbon compounds can be used.
Glucose and fatty acids are the substrates, and either can be used with or without oxygen.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are the substrates, since they are the substances exchanged at the lungs.

questions.stem: Which statement about anaerobic cell respiration in humans is correct?

options.text: Glucose is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide, as it is in yeast cells.
Glucose is converted to lactate and carbon dioxide in the cytoplasm of the cell.
Glucose is converted to lactate, and no carbon dioxide is released at all.
Glucose is converted to lactate using a little oxygen rather than none.

questions.explanation: The word equation is glucose → lactate. Anaerobic respiration in humans uses no oxygen, occurs in the cytoplasm, yields a little ATP and releases no carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: In a respirometer, carbon dioxide is absorbed by potassium hydroxide. With 5.0 g of germinating seeds, the gas volume in the apparatus fell by 1.2 cm³ in 10 minutes. What is the rate of respiration per gram?

options.text: 0.024 cm³ of carbon dioxide produced per gram per minute
0.024 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute
0.12 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute
0.024 cm³ of oxygen given out per gram per minute

questions.explanation: The fall in volume equals the oxygen consumed, because carbon dioxide is removed by the alkali. Rate = 1.2 cm³ ÷ 10 min ÷ 5.0 g = 0.024 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹.

questions.stem: Mature human red blood cells have no mitochondria. Which statement about cell respiration in these cells is correct?

options.text: They cannot respire at all, because all cell respiration takes place in mitochondria.
They respire anaerobically, and so they gain no ATP from the glucose they take up.
They respire anaerobically, releasing ethanol and carbon dioxide into the blood plasma.
They respire anaerobically in the cytoplasm, converting glucose to lactate.

questions.stem: In one reaction of the Krebs cycle, two hydrogen atoms (each with an electron) are removed from a substrate and accepted by NAD. Which statement describes this reaction?

options.text: The substrate is reduced and NAD is oxidized by the transfer.
Neither substance is oxidized, because no oxygen takes part in it.
The substrate is oxidized, but NAD only holds hydrogen and is unchanged.
The substrate has been oxidized and NAD has been reduced.

questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons. Removing hydrogen with its electron (dehydrogenation) oxidizes the substrate, and NAD, which accepts the hydrogen, is reduced; the two occur together as a redox reaction.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly summarises the stages of glycolysis?

options.text: Glucose is phosphorylated using ATP, split into two three-carbon molecules that are oxidized, and ATP is then formed.
Glucose is phosphorylated, forming ATP, and then split into two pyruvate molecules that are reduced.
A single enzyme splits glucose directly into two pyruvate molecules, releasing energy in the form of ATP.
Glucose is split into two pyruvate molecules without any oxidation, as no oxygen is present in the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: During intense exercise, muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate. What is the purpose of this conversion?

options.text: To release extra ATP from pyruvate once the mitochondria have stopped working.
To oxidize pyruvate so that more reduced NAD is available to the cell.
To regenerate NAD so that glycolysis can continue producing ATP.
To convert pyruvate into a form able to enter the mitochondria.

questions.explanation: Reducing pyruvate to lactate converts reduced NAD back to NAD. This allows glycolysis, which needs NAD for its oxidation step, to continue with a net yield of two ATP per glucose.

questions.stem: How does anaerobic cell respiration in yeast differ from anaerobic cell respiration in human muscle?

options.text: Yeast uses a different pathway from glucose to pyruvate, with its own distinct set of enzymes.
Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol only, since carbon dioxide cannot form without oxygen.
There is no difference: both convert pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide when oxygen is absent.
Yeast regenerates NAD by turning pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide, not lactate.

questions.stem: What happens to pyruvate in the link reaction of aerobic cell respiration?

options.text: It enters the Krebs cycle directly, where it combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
It is oxidized and decarboxylated to a 2C acetyl group, which coenzyme A carries to the Krebs cycle.
It reacts with oxygen in the matrix, forming carbon dioxide and a two-carbon acetyl group that enters the cycle.
It is bound by coenzyme A, the enzyme that catalyses its conversion into citrate in the matrix.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Krebs cycle is correct?

options.text: Oxaloacetate is used up in each turn of the cycle, so it must be supplied continually from pyruvate.
Most of the ATP from aerobic respiration is formed directly by the reactions of the cycle itself.
Citrate (6C) forms when an acetyl group (2C) joins oxaloacetate (4C), which is then regenerated.
Carbon dioxide is released when oxygen combines with the carbon atoms of citrate.

questions.explanation: Citrate is produced by transfer of the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate. The cycle's oxidations and decarboxylations then convert citrate back to oxaloacetate, ready for the next acetyl group.
